title: When Every Group Wins but the Average Loses: Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Imagine that Hospital A has a higher survival rate than Hospital B for both mild and severe cases. It seems obvious that Hospital A must also have a higher survival rate overall.
Surprisingly, that conclusion can be wrong.
This phenomenon is called Simpson’s paradox: a relationship that appears within multiple groups can disappear or reverse when the groups are combined. It feels unintuitive because we expect an overall average to preserve a pattern found in every subgroup. However, an average depends not only on the outcomes within each group, but also on how heavily each group is represented.

title: When Every Group Wins but the Average Loses: Simpson’s Paradox
text:
A Hospital Example
Consider the following hypothetical data:








Patient group
Hospital A
Hospital B




Mild cases
90 of 100 survive (90%)
760 of 900 survive (84.4%)


Severe cases
300 of 900 survive (33.3%)
30 of 100 survive (30%)


All cases
390 of 1,000 survive (39%)
790 of 1,000 survive (79%)



Hospital A has the higher survival rate within both groups. Nevertheless, Hospital B has a much higher overall survival rate.
The following graph makes the reversal visible:





Survival rates by patient group and hospital

title: When Every Group Wins but the Average Loses: Simpson’s Paradox
section: Where Does the Reversal Come From?
text:
Where Does the Reversal Come From?
There is no mathematical contradiction. Hospital A treats mostly severe cases, while Hospital B treats mostly mild cases. Because severe cases are less likely to survive regardless of the hospital, Hospital A’s overall rate is pulled downward.
An overall survival rate is a weighted average:
$$ r_{} ===================
w_{}r_{} + w_{}r_{}. $$
Here, (r) represents a group’s survival rate and (w) represents that group’s share of the hospital’s patients.
For Hospital A:
\[
0.10(0.90)+0.90(0.333)\approx 0.39.
\]
For Hospital B:
\[
0.90(0.844)+0.10(0.30)\approx 0.79.
\]
The two overall rates use very different weights. Hospital A’s average is dominated by severe cases, whereas Hospital B’s average is dominated by mild cases. The aggregate comparison therefore mixes together two separate questions: how successfully each hospital treats a given type of patient, and what types of patients each hospital receives.

title: When Every Group Wins but the Average Loses: Simpson’s Paradox
section: Why Economists and Data Scientists Should Care
text:
Why Economists and Data Scientists Should Care
Simpson’s paradox illustrates the importance of confounding variables. A confounding variable is related both to the comparison being made and to the outcome being studied. Here, illness severity is related to hospital choice and to the probability of survival. Ignoring severity produces a misleading comparison.
Similar reversals appear in economics. A region’s average wage can rise even if wages fall within every occupation, provided that employment shifts toward higher-paying occupations. A university can have a lower overall admission rate while having higher admission rates within individual departments. An investment strategy may appear successful in aggregate only because it was used more often during favorable market conditions.
However, the lesson is not simply to divide data into as many groups as possible. Whether we should control for a variable depends on the question and the causal relationships among variables. If illness severity existed before hospital selection, adjusting for it may create a fairer comparison. Controlling for a variable caused by the treatment itself, however, could hide part of the treatment’s true effect.

title: When Every Group Wins but the Average Loses: Simpson’s Paradox
text:
The Main Lesson
Whenever an average is presented, we should ask:
An average of what, and with what weights?
Aggregated statistics are not necessarily incorrect, but they may answer a different question from the one we care about. Simpson’s paradox reminds us that data do not interpret themselves. Good analysis requires understanding how the data were generated, identifying relevant subgroups, and deciding which comparisons are genuinely meaningful.

title: Do Teams That Score More Goals Win More Games in the NHL?
text:
When looking at a hockey team’s performance, one of the first statistics people notice is how many goals the team scores. It seems reasonable to think that teams that score more goals should also win more games. But scoring is only one side of the game. A team can score a lot and still give up just as many goals.
This made me interested in a simple question: Does scoring more goals actually lead to a higher winning percentage in the NHL? I also wanted to see whether goal differential, which takes both scoring and goals allowed into account, gives us a better picture of team performance.
To answer this question, I used rvest in R to scrape historical NHL team statistics from Scrape This Site. The site is a public web-scraping sandbox, so the data can be accessed without a login, CAPTCHA, or paywall.

title: Do Teams That Score More Goals Win More Games in the NHL?
text:
When looking at a hockey team’s performance, one of the first statistics people notice is how many goals the team scores. It seems reasonable to think that teams that score more goals should also win more games. But scoring is only one side of the game. A team can score a lot and still give up just as many goals.
This made me interested in a simple question: Does scoring more goals actually lead to a higher winning percentage in the NHL? I also wanted to see whether goal differential, which takes both scoring and goals allowed into account, gives us a better picture of team performance.
To answer this question, I used rvest in R to scrape historical NHL team statistics from Scrape This Site. The site is a public web-scraping sandbox, so the data can be accessed without a login, CAPTCHA, or paywall.

title: Do Teams That Score More Goals Win More Games in the NHL?
Do Teams That Score More Goals Win More Games in the NHL?
text:
Cleaning the Data
The information collected from the website is initially stored as text. Before doing any calculations, I converted the numerical columns into numbers. I also created a new variable called goal_diff, which is goals scored minus goals allowed.

hockey <- hockey_raw |>
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(year),
    wins = as.numeric(wins),
    losses = as.numeric(losses),
    win_pct = as.numeric(win_pct),
    goals_for = as.numeric(goals_for),
    goals_against = as.numeric(goals_against),
    goal_diff = goals_for - goals_against
  ) |>
  drop_na()

head(hockey)

# A tibble: 6 × 8
  team               year  wins losses win_pct goals_for goals_against goal_diff
  <chr>             <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>         <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Boston Bruins      1990    44     24   0.55        299           264        35
2 Buffalo Sabres     1990    31     30   0.388       292           278        14
3 Calgary Flames     1990    46     26   0.575       344           263        81
4 Chicago Blackhaw…  1990    49     23   0.613       284           211        73
5 Detroit Red Wings  1990    34     38   0.425       273           298       -25
6 Edmonton Oilers    1990    37     37   0.463       272           272         0


A positive goal differential means that a team scored more goals than it allowed during that season, while a negative number means the opposite.

title: Do Teams That Score More Goals Win More Games in the NHL?
text:
Goals Scored and Winning Percentage
First, I compared total goals scored with winning percentage.

ggplot(hockey, aes(x = goals_for, y = win_pct)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Goals Scored and NHL Winning Percentage",
    x = "Goals Scored",
    y = "Winning Percentage"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









The graph shows a positive relationship between scoring and winning percentage. Teams that score more goals generally tend to win a larger share of their games. However, the points are fairly spread out around the trend line. Teams with similar numbers of goals can still have noticeably different winning percentages.
This makes sense because goals scored ignore what happens on defense. Scoring 250 goals is much less impressive if a team also allows 260.

title: Do Teams That Score More Goals Win More Games in the NHL?
text:
Is Goal Differential More Useful?
Next, I compared goal differential with winning percentage.

ggplot(hockey, aes(x = goal_diff, y = win_pct)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Goal Differential and NHL Winning Percentage",
    x = "Goal Differential",
    y = "Winning Percentage"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









The relationship here is much clearer. Teams with large positive goal differentials tend to have higher winning percentages, while teams that allow substantially more goals than they score tend to have lower winning percentages.
To make the comparison more direct, I calculated the correlations between the two measures and winning percentage.

comparison <- tibble(
  measure = c("Goals Scored", "Goal Differential"),
  correlation_with_win_pct = c(
    cor(hockey$goals_for, hockey$win_pct),
    cor(hockey$goal_diff, hockey$win_pct)
  )
)

comparison

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  measure           correlation_with_win_pct
  <chr>                                <dbl>
1 Goals Scored                         0.480
2 Goal Differential                    0.887


The correlation values give a simple way to compare the two relationships. A larger positive correlation means that the statistic moves more closely with winning percentage.In this dataset, the correlation between goals scored and winning percentage is about 0.48, while the correlation between goal differential and winning percentage is about 0.89. This suggests that goal differential is much more closely associated with winning percentage than scoring alone.

title: Do Teams That Score More Goals Win More Games in the NHL?
text:
A Practical Example
To see what successful seasons tend to look like, I also looked at the team-seasons with the highest winning percentages in the scraped data.

top_seasons <- hockey |>
  arrange(desc(win_pct)) |>
  select(
    team,
    year,
    wins,
    losses,
    win_pct,
    goals_for,
    goals_against,
    goal_diff
  ) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

This table makes it possible to look beyond scoring alone. A high-performing team does not simply need to produce goals; the difference between goals scored and goals allowed is also important.

title: Do Teams That Score More Goals Win More Games in the NHL?
text:
Takeaway
The scraped NHL data support the basic idea that scoring more goals is associated with winning more games, but goals scored alone do not tell the whole story. Goal differential gives a more complete measure because it includes both offense and defense.
If I wanted to quickly compare two NHL teams based on a small number of statistics, I would look at goal differential before looking only at total goals scored. A team that scores frequently but also allows many goals may not perform as well as its offensive numbers initially suggest.
This does not mean goal differential explains everything about winning. Team quality also depends on factors such as goaltending, special teams, injuries, and the strength of opponents. In addition, this is a descriptive analysis, so the relationship should not be interpreted as proof that increasing goal differential by a certain amount directly causes a specific increase in winning percentage.
Still, the analysis gives a useful practical rule: when evaluating overall team performance, considering both sides of scoring provides more information than focusing on offense alone. Web scraping made it possible to collect the historical team statistics across many pages and turn them into a dataset that can answer this question directly.

title: The College Wage Premium: Large, but Not Steadily Growing
text:
Does a college degree provide a larger wage advantage today than it did two decades ago? This question matters for understanding both education and inequality. A large wage gap does not necessarily mean that the gap is growing, or that graduates are experiencing strong wage growth.
Using IPUMS Current Population Survey (CPS) microdata, I examine the college wage premium among workers aged 25–54 in May of each year from 2003 through 2024. Three visualizations tell a consistent story: the education wage gap remains substantial, but its evolution is uneven and differs between men and women.

title: The College Wage Premium: Large, but Not Steadily Growing
text:
Data and Measurement
The analysis includes 171,391 person-month observations with at least a high-school diploma. I exclude self-employed workers and observations without valid positive earnings or usual working hours.
The high-school comparison group includes workers whose highest qualification is a high-school diploma or equivalent, with no college education.
Hourly earnings equal weekly earnings divided by usual hours at the main job. This measure includes both hourly and salaried employees. I adjust earnings to May 2024 dollars using the BLS Consumer Price Index.
All medians use EARNWT, the CPS earnings-study weight. These weights make the estimates reflect the represented population rather than treating every sample observation equally. The results describe May snapshots, not annual averages.

title: The College Wage Premium: Large, but Not Steadily Growing
section: 1. The Education Wage Gap Remains Large
text:
1. The Education Wage Gap Remains Large








Figure 1: Weighted median real hourly earnings by education, May 2003–2024.





Workers with a bachelor’s degree or higher consistently earn more than the other groups. In 2024, their median hourly earnings were $38.00, compared with $21.65 for high-school graduates and $24.05 for workers with some college or an associate degree.
However, a large gap does not imply strong real wage growth. The college group’s median was already $37.65 in 2003, measured in the same dollars. The high-school median was $21.98. Both endpoints show relatively little change in purchasing power.

title: The College Wage Premium: Large, but Not Steadily Growing
text:
2. Has the College Premium Increased?
I calculate the college wage premium as:
\[
\text{College premium}
=
\left(
\frac{\text{Median hourly earnings: bachelor's or higher}}
{\text{Median hourly earnings: high school}}
-1
\right)\times 100.
\]








Figure 2: College wage premium calculated from weighted median hourly earnings.





The premium increased from 71.3% in 2003 to 75.5% in 2024. However, the path was not steadily upward: it reached 84.5% in 2022 before declining.
The spike around 2020 also deserves caution. Changes in who remains employed can increase observed median earnings even without individual workers receiving raises. These repeated cross-sections do not measure the same workers’ wage growth.
The endpoint comparison is sensitive to the sample definition. Among workers usually working at least 35 hours per week, the premium changed from 71.9% to 70.4%. The lasting education gap is therefore clearer than evidence of a widening gap.

title: The College Wage Premium: Large, but Not Steadily Growing
section: 3. Different Patterns for Men and Women
text:
3. Different Patterns for Men and Women








Figure 3: Within-sex college wage premiums in May 2003 and May 2024.





The women’s premium rose from 76.1% to 82.1%, while the men’s premium declined from 71.5% to 66.7%.
A higher women’s premium does not mean women earn more than men. Each comparison uses high-school graduates of the same sex as its reference group. Occupation, experience, and employment selection could contribute to these differences.

title: The College Wage Premium: Large, but Not Steadily Growing
text:
Limitations and Takeaway
These are descriptive wage gaps, not causal estimates of attending college. The college group includes graduate degrees, and its composition can change over time. The analysis also excludes workers with missing earnings or variable usual hours.
CPS earnings rounding and topcoding changed in 2023–2024. I use the harmonized rounded series and a common weekly cap of $2,884.61; this cap leaves the overall education-group medians unchanged. Imputed earnings remain included because allocation flags were not downloaded.
Finally, single-month estimates contain sampling noise, and I have not estimated confidence intervals. Small changes should not be interpreted as statistically established differences.
The main finding is an enduring college wage advantage, rather than a steadily growing one. Its apparent change depends on which workers we compare.

title: The College Wage Premium: Large, but Not Steadily Growing

Code and Reproducibility
The GitHub repository contains the complete Quarto source, saved figures, result tables, and a README with data-download and replication instructions. All figures and reported statistics are generated from code. Obtain the original microdata through IPUMS CPS using the sample and variable selections documented in the README.
